chapters.t: The Dream Invitation from an Unnamed Planet
chapters.s: The unnamed-planet sequence opens as a dream of a spotless future built by erasing grief, history and names. Ba, Ananya and Meera turn that promise into a test of consent and dignity: the group will cross the glowing boundary only if it can return carrying a name.

chapters.t: Kabaddi Among Planets in a Dream
chapters.s: As soon as the line glowed, the shadows of the children descended upon the unnamed planet of the dream. Their bodies remained on Earth beside the stump; the journey belonged only to consciousness. From beyond the crack came the smell of water. For the first time, Earth’s water entered the memoryless planet of the dream. The game was not over; the reading of names had begun.

chapters.t: The Lesson of Names on the Unnamed Planet
chapters.s: Beyond the crack was a vast hall. The walls bore only numbers: 30, 300, 791, 0. The planet was not destroyed after the reading of names. Only its brilliance fell away, revealing ordinary grey soil underneath. The moment memory returned, the utopia ended; only then did the possibility of life begin.

Aruni woke with a start. The first light of dawn lay on the bark of the stump; the phone screen was dark, the register open. Dew shone on the new shoot rising from the Channa stump. Beneath it Ananya wrote: “We choose Earth—because it is here that we must answer.”

Ananya first touched the bark of the stump. Its wet roughness settled into her palm as though stories from many years had taken her hand in a single touch. And the first sound of that next voice rose beneath the shade of the new shoot, on the kabaddi ground, from a child: “I am on Earth.” Another child answered, “Present.” A third said, “The watch begins.” And the stump of the Channa tree…

People say a seed is small. But a seed is not small—in a seed an entire tree is hidden, and in the tree an entire village. Before dawn, Ananya opened a new page of the register and wrote the heading: “The Theft of the Seed.” Her hand trembled, but the letters were clear. The watch had now travelled from names to seeds…

The one who steals seed does not steal a field—he steals the future. The field remains where it was, the soil remains where it was; what is carried away is tomorrow's plate. No one had an answer. The fields were divided by debt, chemicals, acquisition, flood, drought and caste. The soil itself was asking: where will you save me? Ananya opened the next page of the register and wrote the title…

The soil opens its mouth when it is asked: where shall I grow? Until then it remains silent, because people have always demanded from it and almost never asked it anything. Ananya opened the register. “The seed has found a place to grow,” she wrote, “but now the crocodile of ownership has climbed onto the embankment.” Dhirmati clenched a handful of soil in her fist.…

Soil holds names; water holds movement. A footfall on soil leaves a mark. That night the children drew a new kabaddi circle around the ring of water. Soil had opened its mouth; water had given its memory. Now the market would try to fit a cap over water's mouth.

People think that once something is burned, the matter is over. But the smell of what burned remains in the air, and smell cannot be locked away. Thus the witness of fire did not end. It became ash upon their heads, light in the letters on the stones, and went out to make air speak. The paper burned to erase memory had turned memory into smoke and spread it through all of Garh Narikel.

Soil, seed, water and fire—all can be taken into the hand. Air cannot. The children tightened the circle of stones. Far, very far away, inside the shining dome in the New Horizon advertisement, a fine crack appeared—perhaps Earth's air had reached there too.

When the sky becomes empty, it is not relief—it is the greatest question of all. A small sky causes fear; the whole sky demands an answer. The chapter did not end with that tremor. It was the first invitation from below: when memory reaches the sky, the roots demand an answer from within the earth.

A lie finds a body at once—file, seal, contract, tender, stage, donation deed. The moment it is written, it puts on a body. The ninth watch of night did not end with that sentence. The watch over the body of the word had only begun. And the next morning Garh Narikel would have to understand that a contract is written not merely on paper but upon whose bones, land, water…

The same word may be written in three places—in the mouth of a dead person's family, on a government flag, and on the wall of a planet with no name. The letters may be identical in all three places. That night there was no laughter from inside the Channa stump, only a grave sound, as though a page of the Tattvacintamani were turning somewhere far away. Gangesha's shadow, Old Budhba's Ghost, the submarine, Meera, Devika, Satyavrat…

A voice is part of the body. It rises from the chest, takes shape in the throat, and the moment it leaves the mouth people think it has become air—belonging to anyone. The chapter did not end that night. The voice had been guarded, but the next danger was approaching with its mouth bound shut—for when a voice cannot be imprisoned, power will try to guard language, printing and reading instead.…

One silence protects power; another covers the soul. One is the companion of crime; the other a bandage over a wound. From inside the stump came only this reply, very faint, like the sound of a leaf's shadow: “Look, but do not devour.” The inheritance of silence did not end here; it had opened the road toward the eye.

A name once heard creates a debt, and no funeral rite can settle that debt—only repayment can. Once a name has entered the ear, an account has opened; now it will be settled not by flowers and garlands but by action. Thus the thirteenth watch did not end. The debt of memory stood on the threshold of the coming day. The green point of the Channa stump shone through the night, and each flash asked: you have heard the name—what will you do now?

The first right over a body belongs to the person who inhabits it. If they wish to speak, their words travel with them; if they do not wish to speak, their silence belongs to them too. The Channa stump remained warm for a long time at that question. The children slept, but the page of the Code of the Body stayed open.

Where an employer is afraid of names, he writes numbers instead. “Men forty-seven, women nine”—this is not a count of human beings; it is a curtain placed where names should be. When everyone had gone, the stump's shade grew longer. Among the stones bearing workers' names, one blank stone was placed: “For the one who works but is not seen.” Touching it, Ananya said…

Justice is no longer allowed to remain an abstraction of files, seals and dates. The chapter asks what justice means for bodies marked by sweat, crushed labour and missing names, then moves toward a ‘body of justice’ grounded in compassion, rules, courage and responsibility.
